absent: Locking and update protocol for the capability pointer table, compat hwcap words, non-global mapping flag, per-CPU vector pointers, mismatch enable flag, static branch key and 32-bit CPU mask.
Command-line or early-boot handling that sets the mismatched 32-bit EL0 enable, enables the static key, and populates the 32-bit mask.
Full contents of the fourth memory-model table beyond its first entry and of cache, override and control-register tables named but not shown in this lane.
Decoding, sanitization and cross-CPU merge algorithm that consumes the feature tables and maintains the system capability bitmap.
Semantics of conditional visibility helpers and rationale for individual safe fallback values beyond the listed defaults.

findings.text: The default 32-bit compat hwcap value combines seven capability members covering halfword support, Thumb, fast multiply, DSP extensions, TLS, hardware divide and large physical addressing, and serves as the initial value for the first compat hwcap word.

Three unsigned compat hwcap words are held in read-mostly storage; the first is preinitialized to the default set while the other two start zeroed, indicating early setup followed by predominantly read access.

A static table indexed by capability number holds pointers to constant capability descriptors, sized by the total capability count and marked read-only after init, indicating it is populated during initialization and thereafter treated as immutable.
A global boolean controlling non-global mappings lives in read-mostly storage and defaults to disabled.
Each CPU keeps a read-mostly pointer to its current exception vector description, initialized to the default vectors symbol, so the vector can vary per CPU while remaining rarely written.
Heterogeneous 32-bit EL0 support uses a static read-mostly enable flag defaulting off, a static branch key defaulting false, and a static read-mostly CPU mask identifying 32-bit-capable CPUs.
A global no-argument diagnostic routine reports the system-wide capability bitmap at emergency log level, with a standard prefix added by file-wide logging setup.

ID field matchers bind a system register with field position, width, signedness and an allowed value interval. Positive features match from a named minimum up to the widest representable positive value, accounting for signed versus unsigned encoding; reverse-polarity features match from the minimum negative value up to a named maximum.

A feature-field descriptor records signedness, user visibility, cross-CPU strictness, safety direction, bit position, bit width and a safe fallback value. Unsigned and signed constructors select the signedness; a terminator is recognized by zero width.

Instruction-feature tables for four ID registers enumerate mostly four-bit fields with per-field visibility, strictness, safety direction and safe value, closed by a terminator. Early tables are broadly visible strict lower-safe; pointer-authentication fields become visible only when that support is enabled and use exact matching; newer tables mix nonstrict lower-safe entries with hidden strict entries.

Processor-feature and SVE-feature tables follow the same descriptor pattern. Processor tables hide most maintenance, virtualization and exception-level fields while exposing selected items such as data-independent timing, SVE, memory tagging, branch target identification and guarded control stack conditionally on build options; SVE extension fields are conditionally visible strict lower-safe; signed descriptors use not-implemented safe values for floating-point, SIMD and related fields.

Matrix, floating-point and memory-model tables use the same pattern with narrower widths where architecturally defined. Matrix and floating-point extension fields use strict exact matching with conditional visibility for matrix; memory tables hide most fields, expose enhanced counter virtualization, alternate float handling, address translation and permission-overlay items, treat stage-two granules as exact nonstrict with safe fallback set, stage-one granules and physical range as nonstrict lower-safe, and use higher-safe only for the speculative error field.

Stage-two granule size advertising is not reconciled across CPUs; inconsistent values are treated as a reason to avoid KVM rather than corrected. Non-configured page-size mismatches and differing physical address ranges are tolerated as nonstrict, assuming mappings stay within the minimum range and the configured page size remains universally supported.
Emergency logging relies on an external print helper owned by another dossier.
